
graceDR randomizes clinical trial participants one at a time into two or more arms. It uses
a modified minimal sufficient balance (MSB) algorithm with weighted balance variables, an
exact-allocation run-in, and forced allocation at chosen enrollment totals. The trial lives
in one encrypted file, every change is written to an audit log, and any past assignment can
be replayed.

This vignette walks through a small made-up trial of 40 participants.

## Install

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
pak::pak("BiostatDoc/grace")
```

```{r setup}
library(graceDR)
```

## Describe the design

A design lists the number of participants, the balance variables, the arms, and the
allocation ratio. `example_design()` builds a small one with two arms (`A` and `B`) in a 1:1
ratio and balance variables `sex`, `race`, and `age`.

```{r design}
design <- example_design(40)
design
```

The run-in is the first stretch of enrollment where counts are held to exact targets. The
checkpoints show the group sizes the algorithm will reach exactly.

## Choose a passphrase

The trial file is encrypted with a passphrase that grace reads from the `GRACE_PASSPHRASE`
environment variable. This vignette sets it in the code only because the data are made up.

```{r passphrase}
Sys.setenv(GRACE_PASSPHRASE = "vignette-only")
```

For a real trial, never write the passphrase in a script. Keep it in your `.Renviron` file
or in a `.env` file that is listed in `.gitignore`, and keep a copy in a password manager.
Nobody can read the trial file without it.

## Create the trial

`create_trial()` writes the encrypted file. The seed makes the random draws reproducible, and
the optional codes file lists the treatment codes to hand out, one set per arm. The package
ships a made-up codes file.

```{r create}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
codes_file <- system.file("extdata", "example_codes.csv", package = "graceDR")
create_trial(path, design, seed = 20260611, codes = codes_file)
```

## Randomize participants

`example_participants` holds 40 made-up participants. Each call to `randomize()` assigns one
participant, saves the record and an audit row, and returns the assignment.

```{r randomize}
head(example_participants)

assignments <- vector("list", nrow(example_participants))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(example_participants))) {
  participant <- example_participants[j, ]
  assignments[[j]] <- randomize(
    path,
    participant$id,
    participant[c("sex", "race", "age")]
  )
}
assignments[[1]]
```

Each assignment records the probabilities that were used and the phase of the algorithm:
`runin`, `quota`, `bound`, `msb-biased`, or `msb-random`.

```{r phases}
table(vapply(assignments, \(assignment) assignment$phase, character(1)))
```

## Check the balance

`trial_status()` reads the file without randomizing anyone. It reports group sizes, balance
tables, and standardized mean differences (SMDs), with two plots.

```{r status}
status <- trial_status(path)
status$group_sizes
status$balance
```

Categorical variables show a count and percentage in each arm. Continuous variables show the
mean and standard deviation.

The first plot shows how far each arm is from its target size as enrollment goes on. The
second shows the largest SMD for each balance variable.

```{r imbalance-plot}
status$imbalance_plot
```

```{r smd-plot}
status$smd_plot
```

The report can be narrowed with `from`, `to`, `checkpoint`, and `vars`. For example, the
balance at the end of the run-in:

```{r run-in}
trial_status(path, checkpoint = "run-in")$group_sizes
```

## Override an assignment

Sometimes the unblinded statistician must change an assignment, for example after a data
entry error. `override_assignment()` is the only supported way to do it. It requires a
reason, voids the old treatment code, and draws a new one.

```{r override}
current_arm <- assignments[[3]]$arm
new_arm <- setdiff(design$arms, current_arm)
override_assignment(
  path,
  "P003",
  new_arm,
  reason = "Randomized with the wrong race in the example."
)
```

## Read the audit log

Every action is appended to the audit log, and nothing can edit or delete a row.

```{r audit}
log <- audit_log(path)
nrow(log)
tail(log, 3)
```

## Replay assignments

An auditor can redraw any assignment from the stored random number state and compare it with
the record. For an overridden participant the comparison uses the original assignment, which
the audit log keeps.

```{r replay}
replay_assignment(path, "P003")

replays <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(example_participants$id, \(id) replay_assignment(path, id))
)
all(replays$match)
```

## Simulate operating characteristics

Before a trial starts, `simulate_trials()` compares the algorithm with simple random
allocation, permuted blocks, minimization, and unmodified MSB on the same synthetic
participants. This small run uses 20 simulated trials; a real study would use 1000 or more.
Set `parallel = TRUE` after choosing a backend with `future::plan()` to run them in parallel.

```{r simulate}
simulation <- simulate_trials(
  design,
  n_sims = 20,
  generator = example_generator_iid(),
  seed = 1
)
simulation
```

`summary()` gives the mean, standard deviation, 95th and 99th percentiles, and maximum of each
metric over the simulated trials. The upper percentiles show the worst cases.

```{r summary}
results <- summary(simulation)
keep <- results$metric %in% c("smd_max", "correct_guess") & results$point %in% c("end", "all")
results[keep, c("method", "metric", "mean", "q95", "max")]
```

A smaller `smd_max` means better balance, and a `correct_guess` percentage near 50 for two
arms means the next assignment is hard to predict.
